sn54.10:1.3: The several discourses at Kimbilā all feature the monk named Kimila; it is a common practice to this day to name monastics for their place of residence. We might translate, “the venerable of Kimbilā”. In those discourses, he asks the Buddha about the long lasting of the dispensation ([an5.201](), [an6.40](), [an7.59]()).
sn54.10:5.5: This shows how mindfulness of breathing maps on to the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, a theme explored in more detail in [mn118]().
sn54.10:6.4: The “inbreathing” phrase is absent from MS, but it is found in PTS.
sn54.10:6.7: The sense here is that the pleasant feelings of breath meditation are part of the full spectrum of feelings contemplated in _satipaṭṭhāna_, which include painful feelings ([mn10:32.1]()). The meditator “carefully” (_sādhukaṁ_) focuses on these feelings as they manifest in the breath. The point is that “breath” is not purely a physical phenomenon. The material property of “air” is its most obvious dimension, but we experience breath as a complex that includes emotional and cognitive dimensions. As the physical process becomes subtle, feeling becomes apparent as an aspect of the breath that has always been there, but not clearly perceived.
